newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Britain to join euro "early" - Irish premier.
newsitem.headline: Britain to join euro "early" - Irish premier.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said in remarks published on Tuesday that he expected Britain's new Labour government to join European economic and monetary union (EMU) close to its January 1999 start.

Bruton, the first foreign leader to meet British Prime Minister Tony Blair after his May 1 election victory, told the Irish Times that he had no "insider knowlege" on the new British government's intentions.
But he said Blair's government, which has taken a wait-and-see attitude to EMU and promised a referendum before joining, would probably join sooner rather than later.
"I think there is a possibility that Britain might go in earlier rather than later," he told the newspaper.
"The new British government has a more open view on the issue and I think that the objective economic interest of Britain will point in favour of an early rather than a late decision," he said.

Asked if Britain might join from the start, Bruton, who met Blair to discuss Northern Ireland shortly after the May 1 election, replied: "Either that or very early in the new period, that's what I'm talking about. That is my assessment of what I think would be in Britain's interest, I'm not speaking from insider knowledge."
It was the most optimistic statement to date by a member of the current Irish government about the likely plans of its biggest trading partner, Britain, for EMU membership.

Bruton's three-party coalition is fighting June 6 elections against a resurgent opposition led by Fianna Fail, which has an 11 point lead in opinion polls. EMU membership is not a campaign issue as all major parties support it.
Britain's decision is crucial for the Irish economy, because the punt/sterling exchange rate is a key determinant of exports and inflation in Ireland due to the two countries' close trading ties.
Entering EMU without Britain would mean losing any control over the exchange rate against sterling, which some economists say would be dangerous.

Irish exporters have voiced alarm about the prospect of the country joining EMU if Britain remains outside the project but all major political parties say that Dublin will press ahead towards EMU anyway.
Bruton acknowledged that Irish membership of EMU without Britain would be difficult because one third of the nation's trade is with its nearest neighbour.
"There is no doubt about that. The possibility of some shock to our economy coming is much greater if one of our principal trading partners is outside the euro zone," he said.
"It's a difficult choice but I think the right choice is to go into the euro, regardless of what Britain does."
Bruton said Irish EMU membership would help cement trading and other ties with continental Europe. "Our greatest economic interest is with mainland Europe in the longer term."
He said that if Britain failed to join it would make Ireland the only English-speaking nation in the euro zone and give Ireland advantages because the language of international finance is English.

Government officials say that Irish membership of EMU will also attract more foreign investment, which has helped sustain a major economic boom in Ireland over recent years and create jobs at the rate of 1,000 per week.
